lead: A pass transistor uses a MOSFET as a switch: its gate is the control and data flows between its source and drain. An nMOS passes a clean 0 but stops a 1 one threshold below its gate; a pMOS passes a clean 1 but stops a 0 one threshold above ground. A transmission gate (TG) puts an nMOS and a pMOS in parallel with complementary controls, so together they pass both rails. Pass-transistor logic builds multiplexers, XOR gates, latches and adder cells with fewer transistors than static CMOS, at the price of weak levels, charge sharing and the need to restore signals.
prereq: You need: the body effect on threshold voltage (see Threshold voltage and body effect) and static CMOS gates.

sections.h3: The nMOS switch and its threshold drop

blocks.text: Put an nMOS between input A and output Y with its gate at control C = V<sub>DD</sub>. Whichever terminal is at the lower voltage acts as the source.

items: Passing a 0. A = 0 V, Y starts high. A is the source, so VGS = VDD − 0 = VDD for the whole discharge. Y falls all the way to 0 V: a strong 0.
Passing a 1. A = VDD, Y starts at 0 V. Now Y is the source, so VGS = VDD − VY falls as Y rises. The transistor cuts off when VGS reaches Vtn, so Y stops at VDD − Vtn: a weak 1.

blocks.text: The source of this nMOS is Y, which is above the grounded substrate, so V<sub>SB</sub> = V<sub>Y</sub> and the body effect raises the threshold just when it matters:
Vtn = Vt0 + γ(√(2φF + VSB) − √(2φF)) Here vt0 is the zero-bias threshold, γ the body-effect coefficient in V1/2 and 2φF the surface potential term in volts.

Because V<sub>Y</sub> appears on both sides, the final level is found by iteration (worked example 1). A weak 1 is a problem: an inverter driven by it has its pMOS still slightly on, so it draws static current and switches slowly. If a later pass transistor's gate is itself driven by a weak level, the drops add up.

sections.h3: The pMOS switch and the transmission gate

blocks.text: A pMOS switch is the mirror image: with its gate at 0 V it passes a strong 1 but its output can fall only to |V<sub>tp</sub>| above ground, a weak 0.

A transmission gate puts both in parallel: the nMOS gate gets C and the pMOS gate gets C̄, the complement. With C = 1 both can conduct and Y follows A over the full range; with C = 0 both are off and Y is high-impedance (floating). Near 0 V the nMOS carries most of the current and near V<sub>DD</sub> the pMOS does, so the TG's on-resistance stays nearly constant across the swing. The cost is two transistors per switch and a C̄ wire.

2:1 multiplexer. Two TGs share output Y: one passes A when S = 1, the other passes B when S = 0. One of the two is always on, so Y is always driven. It takes 4 transistors plus an inverter for S̄, against 12 for a static CMOS version (an AOI22 gate, an output inverter and a select inverter).

XOR. A TG passes B̄ or B depending on A, giving A ⊕ B with 6 to 8 transistors; full adders built this way are smaller than static ones. Latches use a TG as the input switch and another to close the feedback loop (see Static and dynamic latches and registers).

Complementary pass-transistor logic (CPL) uses nMOS-only networks with both true and complement signals, then restores each output with an inverter; some syllabi list it with PTL. The rules for every pass network: never drive a gate input straight from a long chain of switches, add a restoring inverter after about three or four switches, because delay grows roughly with the square of the chain length (it is an RC ladder, see Elmore delay); and watch for charge sharing when a floating node is connected to another.

examples.question: An nMOS pass transistor has its gate and input at V<sub>DD</sub> = 1.8 V. V<sub>t0</sub> = 0.5 V, γ = 0.4 V<sup>1/2</sup> and 2φ<sub>F</sub> = 0.7 V. Find the highest output level without and with the body effect. What does a transmission gate pass?
steps: With body effect V<sub>Y</sub> = 1.8 − V<sub>tn</sub>(V<sub>Y</sub>). Try V<sub>Y</sub> = 1.30 V: V<sub>tn</sub> = 0.5 + 0.4(√2.0 − √0.7) = 0.5 + 0.4(1.414 − 0.837) = 0.731 V, so V<sub>Y</sub> = 1.069 V.
Try V<sub>Y</sub> = 1.103 V: V<sub>tn</sub> = 0.5 + 0.4(√1.803 − 0.837) = 0.702 V, so V<sub>Y</sub> = 1.098 V. The values have settled: V<sub>Y</sub> ≈ 1.10 V with V<sub>tn</sub> ≈ 0.70 V.
Transmission gate: the pMOS (gate at 0 V, source at 1.8 V) stays on until Y reaches 1.8 V, so Y = 1.8 V.
examples.answer: An nMOS alone passes 1.30 V ignoring body effect and only about 1.10 V with it (V<sub>tn</sub> rises to 0.70 V); the transmission gate passes the full 1.8 V.

examples.question: The weak 1.10 V level drives a CMOS inverter with V<sub>DD</sub> = 1.8 V, k<sub>n</sub> = k<sub>p</sub> = 200 µA/V² and V<sub>tn</sub> = |V<sub>tp</sub>| = 0.5 V. Is the pMOS off? Estimate the static current.
steps: pMOS V<sub>SG</sub> = 1.8 − 1.10 = 0.70 V > |V<sub>tp</sub>| = 0.5 V, so the pMOS is still on, with overdrive 0.20 V.
The nMOS has V<sub>GS</sub> = 1.10 V (overdrive 0.60 V) and pulls the output low, so the pMOS is saturated and limits the current.
I ≈ (200/2)(0.20)² = 100 × 0.04 = 4 µA, flowing all the time the weak 1 is held.
examples.answer: The pMOS stays on and about 4 µA flows from V<sub>DD</sub> to ground, which is why weak levels are restored or a TG is used.

traps: Giving an nMOS switch output of V<sub>DD</sub> for a passed 1. It stops at V<sub>DD</sub> − V<sub>tn</sub>, and V<sub>tn</sub> is raised by the body effect.
Taking the input terminal as the source in every case. The source is whichever terminal is lower; for a passed 1 through an nMOS it is the output.
Driving the TG's pMOS with C. The pMOS gate must get C̄, or the switch never fully opens or closes.
Saying a 2:1 TG multiplexer leaves its output floating. One of its two TGs is always on.
Driving a long chain of switches without a restoring buffer. Delay grows about as the square of the chain length.

quiz.q: An nMOS switch has gate and input at V<sub>DD</sub>. What is its highest output?
quiz.a: V<sub>DD</sub> − V<sub>tn</sub>, with V<sub>tn</sub> raised by the body effect.

quiz.q: Which control signal drives the pMOS of a transmission gate?
quiz.a: C̄, the complement of the control C that drives the nMOS.

quiz.q: Why does a pMOS switch fail to pass a full 0?
quiz.a: As the output falls, it becomes the pMOS source, so V<sub>SG</sub> = V<sub>Y</sub> − 0 shrinks; the device cuts off when V<sub>Y</sub> = |V<sub>tp</sub>|.

quiz.q: Why is a TG's on-resistance nearly constant over the swing?
quiz.a: Near 0 V the nMOS has full overdrive and conducts well, near V<sub>DD</sub> the pMOS does; as one weakens the other strengthens, so their parallel resistance changes little.

quiz.q: An nMOS switch has V<sub>G</sub> = V<sub>in</sub> = 2.5 V and its threshold rises to 0.7 V at the final output level. Find the output.
How many transistors does a TG 2:1 multiplexer need, including the select inverter?
quiz.a: 4 for the two TGs plus 2 for the inverter: 6, against 12 for a static version built from an AOI22 gate and two inverters.

quiz.q: A TG output drives a long wire and then a CMOS gate. Why is a restoring inverter usually added?
quiz.a: The TG has no gain: it passes on whatever level and drive it receives, and its resistance adds to the wire RC. An inverter gives full rails, sharp edges and fresh drive.

beyond: Not for the exam. Standard-cell libraries use transmission gates inside multiplexers, XOR cells and almost every flip-flop. At very low supply voltages the threshold drop of a single nMOS becomes a large fraction of the swing, so nMOS-only pass logic is rarely used in modern processes. Search next for transmission-gate full adders, CPL and charge sharing.
